```text
                    ▼

              Change Control
                    │
                    ▼

                  Review
                    │
                    ▼

           Validation Evidence
                    │
                    ▼

           Governance Decision
                    │
                    ▼

             Version Control
                    │
                    ▼

            Lifecycle Control
                    │
                    ▼

               Preservation

```

Governance therefore ensures that Templates evolve deliberately, remain traceable, and preserve architectural consistency throughout their lifecycle.

### 1.1. Purpose

This document defines the constraint model used by the Templates component of the Documentation Framework.

Template Constraints establish restrictions and conditions that govern the valid structure, composition, relationships, parameters, and applicability of Templates and their Elements.

### 1.3. Architectural Position

Template Constraints are part of the structural definition of a Template.

They refine the Template Model and Template Schema defined by:

* DF-TPL-003 — Template Model;
* DF-TPL-005 — Template Schema.

Constraints provide rules against which conformance may subsequently be evaluated by DF-TPL-007 — Template Validation.

The responsibility boundary is therefore:

```text

            Template Model
            │
            └── defines conceptual structure

            Template Schema
            │
            └── represents structural definition

            Template Constraints
            │
            └── defines restrictions and conditions

            Template Validation
            │
            └── evaluates conformance

```

---

# 3. Constraint Model

A **Template Constraint** is a defined restriction or condition applicable to a Template entity or relationship.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template Constraint
            │
            ├── Target
            │
            ├── Constraint Type
            │
            ├── Rule
            │
            ├── Applicability
            │
            └── Severity

```

A constraint may apply to:

* a Template;
* a Template Structure;
* a Template Section;
* a Template Element;
* a Template Parameter;
* a Template Relationship;
* a Composition;
* a Specialization.

The constraint model defines the semantics of the restriction but does not prescribe how the restriction is implemented.

---

# 4. Constraint Participants

Constraints may target the entities defined by the Template Model.

```text"

            Template
            │
            ├── Template Structure
            │   │
            │   └── Template Section
            │       │
            │       └── Template Element
            │
            ├── Template Parameter
            │
            ├── Template Relationship
            │
            ├── Template Composition
            │
            └── Template Specialization

```

A constraint may apply to a single entity or to a relationship between entities.

---

# 5. Constraint Categories

The principal categories are:

```text

            Template Constraint
            │
            ├── Structural Constraint
            │
            ├── Element Constraint
            │
            ├── Occurrence Constraint
            │
            ├── Cardinality Constraint
            │
            ├── Parameter Constraint
            │
            ├── Relationship Constraint
            │
            ├── Composition Constraint
            │
            ├── Specialization Constraint
            │
            └── Applicability Constraint

```

These categories describe the semantic purpose of a constraint.

They are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

A single constraint may involve more than one aspect of a Template.

---

# 6. Structural Constraints

A **Structural Constraint** restricts the organization of a Template Structure.

Examples include requirements concerning:

* required Sections;
* permitted Elements;
* Section ordering;
* permitted nesting;
* structural dependencies between Sections;
* permitted structural arrangements.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template Structure
            │
            └── Structural Constraints
                │
                ├── required Section
                │
                ├── permitted Element
                │
                └── ordering rule

```

Structural Constraints must remain consistent with the Template Schema.

---

# 8. Occurrence Constraints

An **Occurrence Constraint** controls how many times an Element or Section may occur within a defined structural context.

Typical occurrence semantics include:

```text

0 occurrences
1 occurrence
0..1 occurrences
1..N occurrences
0..N occurrences

```

For example:

```text

            Template Section
            │
            └── contains  ─────►  Element
                                  │
                                  └── occurrence: 1..N

```

Occurrence constraints are structural restrictions.

They must not be interpreted as workflow requirements.

---

# 9. Cardinality Constraints

A **Cardinality Constraint** restricts the number of permitted participants in a relationship.

For example:

```text

            Template A
            │
            └── composes  ─────►  Template B

```

may be constrained so that a particular Template can compose one or more Templates.

Cardinality constraints may apply to:

* Template-to-Template relationships;
* Template-to-Element relationships;
* Element-to-Element relationships;
* containment relationships.

Cardinality semantics must remain consistent with DF-TPL-005 and DF-TPL-009.

---

# 11. Relationship Constraints

A **Relationship Constraint** restricts the permitted use of Template Relationships.

Relationship Constraints may govern:

* permitted relationship types;
* permitted source entities;
* permitted target entities;
* direction;
* cardinality;
* relationship applicability;
* prohibited relationships;
* dependency conditions.

For example:

```text

            Template A
            │
            └── Relationship Constraint
                │
                ├── specialization  ─────►  permitted
                │
                ├── composition     ─────►  permitted
                │
                └── other type      ─────►  restricted

```

Relationship semantics themselves are defined by DF-TPL-009.

---

# 12. Composition Constraints

A **Composition Constraint** restricts how Templates may be composed.

Composition Constraints may define:

* permitted composed Templates;
* prohibited compositions;
* composition cardinality;
* composition applicability;
* structural compatibility requirements;
* composition dependency restrictions.

Composition Constraints must prevent an unrestricted interpretation of Template reuse.

For example:

```text

            Template A
            │
            └── composes  ─────►  Template B

```

may be valid only when the relationship satisfies the applicable Composition Constraints.

---

# 13. Specialization Constraints

A **Specialization Constraint** restricts how a Template may specialize another Template.

Specialization Constraints may define:

* permitted base Templates;
* permitted derived Templates;
* structural compatibility;
* restrictions on inherited structure;
* permitted specialization scope;
* prohibited specialization patterns.

Conceptually:

```text

            Base Template
            │
            └── specialization constraint
                            │
                            ▼

                     Derived Template

```

Specialization Constraints must preserve the semantic distinction between specialization and Template Version.

---

# 14. Applicability Constraints

An **Applicability Constraint** defines the conditions under which a Template entity, Element, Parameter, or Relationship applies.

Applicability may depend on:

* Template context;
* structural context;
* another Template Element;
* a Template Parameter;
* a defined Template Relationship.

Conceptually:

```text

            Element A
            │
            └── applicable when  ─────►  defined condition

```

Applicability Constraints allow controlled structural variation without requiring separate Templates for every possible variation.

---

# 15. Constraint Representation

A Template Constraint should be conceptually representable as:

```text

            Constraint
            │
            ├── Target
            │
            ├── Type
            │
            ├── Rule
            │
            ├── Applicability
            │
            └── Severity

```

Where:

| Property          | Meaning                                                |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Target**        | Entity or relationship to which the constraint applies |
| **Type**          | Semantic category of the constraint                    |
| **Rule**          | Restriction or condition being defined                 |
| **Applicability** | Context in which the rule applies                      |
| **Severity**      | Significance assigned to non-conformance               |

The exact representation may be defined by the Template Schema.

No particular syntax, serialization format, database representation, or programming language is required.

---

# 16. Constraint Scope

A constraint may operate at different structural scopes.

### 16.1. Template Scope

Applies to the Template as a whole.

```text

            Template
            │
            └── Constraint

```

### 16.2. Section Scope

Applies to a Template Section and its contents.

```text

            Template Section
            │
            └── Constraint

```

### 16.3. Element Scope

Applies to an individual Template Element.

```text

            Template Element
            │
            └── Constraint

```

### 16.4. Relationship Scope

Applies to a relationship between participants.

```text

            Entity A
            │
            └── Relationship
                │
                └── Constraint

```

### 16.5. Parameter Scope

Applies to a Template Parameter.

```text

            Template Parameter
            │
            └── Constraint

```

---

---

# 17. Constraint Combination

Multiple constraints may apply to the same Template entity.

For example:

```text

            Template Element
            │
            ├── Element Constraint
            │
            ├── Occurrence Constraint
            │
            ├── Applicability Constraint
            │
            └── Relationship Constraint

```

When multiple constraints apply, their combined interpretation must remain deterministic.

Constraints must not be interpreted in isolation when their scope overlaps.

Conflicting constraints must be identifiable and must not result in an undefined Template interpretation.

---

# 18. Constraint Precedence

When constraints operate at different scopes, their applicability must remain explicit.

For example:

```text

            Template Constraint
            │
            └── Section Constraint
                │
                └── Element Constraint

```

A more specific constraint may refine a broader constraint when such refinement is explicitly permitted.

A specific constraint must not silently override a broader constraint when the resulting interpretation would violate the Template Model.

Detailed precedence rules may be refined by future Template Constraint specifications.

---

# 19. Constraint and Validation

Template Constraints define the conditions for permitted Template structures.

Template Validation evaluates whether those conditions are satisfied.

Therefore:

```text

            Constraint
            │
            └── defines  ─────►  permitted condition

            Validation
            │
            └── evaluates  ─────►  actual conformance

```

A constraint does not itself produce a validation result.

Validation may classify a Template as:

* Conformant;
* Non-Conformant;
* Indeterminate.

These results are defined by DF-TPL-007.

---

# 22. Constraint and Template Version

Constraints are interpreted within the context of the Template Version in which they are defined.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template
            │
            └── Version
                │
                └── Constraints

```

A change to a constraint may therefore constitute a Template Version change.

Template Version remains distinct from:

* Document Edition;
* Document Revision;
* Document Baseline;
* Document Instance.

---

# 23. Constraint and Relationships

Constraints may restrict the relationships defined by DF-TPL-009.

For example:

```text

            Template A
            │
            └── Relationship
                │
                └── Relationship Constraint

```

Relationship Constraints may restrict:

* participant types;
* direction;
* cardinality;
* applicability;
* composition;
* specialization.

Constraints must not redefine relationship categories.

---

# 24. Constraint and Metadata, Identity, and Classification

Templates may define structural locations for Metadata, Document Identity, and Classification information.

Constraints may therefore establish requirements concerning those locations.

However, Templates do not redefine the semantics of those components.

The responsibility boundary remains:

```text

            Metadata
            │
            └── defines metadata semantics

            Document Identity
            │
            └── defines identity semantics

            Classification
            │
            └── defines classification semantics

            Templates
            │
            └── define structural requirements

```

Compatibility constraints may therefore reference these components without incorporating their responsibilities into Templates.

---

# 26. Constraint Invariants

The following invariants apply to Template Constraints.

### 26.1. Invariant 1 — Explicit Target

Every constraint must have an identifiable target.

### 26.2. Invariant 2 — Explicit Semantics

Every constraint must define the restriction or condition it establishes.

### 26.3. Invariant 3 — Defined Scope

The applicability scope of a constraint must be determinable.

### 26.4. Invariant 4 — Structural Consistency

Constraints must remain consistent with the Template Model and Template Schema.

### 26.5. Invariant 5 — No Implicit Override

A constraint must not silently override another applicable constraint.

### 26.6. Invariant 6 — Validation Separation

Constraints define conditions; validation evaluates conformance.

### 26.7. Invariant 7 — Version Traceability

Constraint changes must be attributable to the applicable Template Version.

### 26.8. Invariant 8 — Responsibility Separation

Constraints must not redefine concepts owned by other Documentation Framework components.

### 26.9. Invariant 9 — Technology Independence

Constraint semantics must not depend on a specific implementation technology.

### 26.10. Invariant 10 — Deterministic Interpretation

Applicable constraints must produce an unambiguous structural interpretation.

# 28. Constraint Model Summary

Template Constraints provide the formal mechanism for restricting the structures and relationships defined by Templates.

The principal categories are:

```text

            Template Constraint
            │
            ├── Structural Constraint
            │
            ├── Element Constraint
            │
            ├── Occurrence Constraint
            │
            ├── Cardinality Constraint
            │
            ├── Parameter Constraint
            │
            ├── Relationship Constraint
            │
            ├── Composition Constraint
            │
            ├── Specialization Constraint
            │
            └── Applicability Constraint

```

The fundamental distinction is:

```text

    Template Model
        ─────►  defines what exists

    Template Schema
        ─────►  defines how it is structurally represented

    Template Constraints
        ─────►  define what is permitted

    Template Validation
        ─────►  determines whether the definition conforms

```

This separation provides an explicit and technology-independent foundation for controlled Template structures, reuse, specialization, composition, and evolution.

### 1.1. Purpose

This document defines the extensibility model of the Templates component of the Documentation Framework.

Template Extensibility establishes how Templates may be extended, specialized, composed, parameterized, and otherwise evolved while preserving the semantic and architectural integrity of the Documentation Framework.

### 1.3. Architectural Position

Template Extensibility provides mechanisms for adapting existing Template definitions without requiring every variation to be defined independently.

The extensibility model builds upon:

* Template Specialization;
* Template Composition;
* Template Parameterization;
* reusable Template Elements;
* Template Relationships;
* Template Constraints.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template Extensibility
            │
            ├── Specialization
            │
            ├── Composition
            │
            ├── Parameterization
            │
            ├── Element Reuse
            │
            └── Controlled Extension

```

---

# 3. Extensibility Principles

Template extensibility is governed by the following principles.

### 3.1. Reuse

Existing Templates and Template Elements should be reused whenever they provide the required semantics.

### 3.2. Explicit Extension

Every extension must have an explicit semantic basis.

Implicit modifications are not considered valid extensibility mechanisms.

### 3.3. Controlled Variation

Variation must be controlled through defined extensibility mechanisms.

### 3.4. Semantic Preservation

An extension must preserve the semantics of the entities it extends unless the extension mechanism explicitly permits semantic specialization.

### 3.5. Separation of Responsibilities

Extensibility must not transfer responsibilities between Documentation Framework components.

### 3.6. Technology Independence

Extensibility must remain independent of implementation technology.

### 3.7. Traceability

Extensions must remain traceable to their source Templates, Elements, or definitions.

### 3.8. Controlled Evolution

Extensions must support controlled evolution and compatibility assessment.

---

# 4. Extensibility Mechanisms

The principal extensibility mechanisms are:

```text

            Template Extensibility
            │
            ├── Specialization
            │
            ├── Composition
            │
            ├── Parameterization
            │
            ├── Element Reuse
            │
            └── Structural Extension

```

These mechanisms may be used independently or in combination when their semantics are compatible.

---

# 5. Template Specialization

Template Specialization provides a mechanism for deriving a more specific Template from an existing Template.

Conceptually:

```text

            Base Template
            │
            └── specializes
                     │
                     ▼

            Specialized Template

```

A specialized Template remains related to its base Template through a Specialization Relationship.

Specialization may provide:

* additional structural requirements;
* more specific Elements;
* restricted applicability;
* domain-specific structure;
* additional constraints.

Specialization must not be used merely to represent a new Version of the same Template.

---

# 6. Template Composition

Template Composition provides a mechanism for constructing a Template from reusable Template structures.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template A
            │
            ├── composes  ─────►  Template B
            │
            └── composes  ─────►  Template C

```

Composed Templates may contribute reusable:

* Structures;
* Sections;
* Elements;
* Parameters;
* defined structural patterns.

Composition promotes reuse without requiring structural duplication.

Composition does not imply specialization.

---

# 7. Template Parameterization

Template Parameterization allows a Template to contain explicitly defined parameters that control permitted variation.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template
            │
            └── Parameter
                │
                └── controls  ─────►  Template variation

```

Parameters may influence:

* optional Elements;
* structural alternatives;
* applicability;
* reusable content structures;
* permitted configuration choices.

Parameter definitions belong to the Template.

Parameter values belong to a Template Instance.

Therefore:

```text

            Template
            │
            └── defines  ─────►  Parameter

            Template Instance
            │
            └── supplies  ─────►  Parameter Value

```

---

# 8. Element Reuse

Template Elements may be reused by multiple Templates.

Conceptually:

```text

            Reusable Element
            │
            ├───────►  Template A
            │
            ├───────►  Template B
            │
            └───────►  Template C

```

Reuse may reduce duplication and improve consistency.

A reused Element must retain its defined semantics.

Templates may establish additional constraints on the context in which the Element is used, subject to the applicable Template Constraints.

---

# 9. Structural Extension

A Template may be extended by adding additional structural components.

For example:

```text

            Base Template
            │
            ├── Section A
            │
            └── Section B

            Extended Template
            │
            ├── Section A
            │
            ├── Section B
            │
            └── Section C

```

Structural extension may occur through specialization or another explicitly defined extensibility mechanism.

An extension must not silently modify the meaning of existing structural components.

---

# 10. Controlled Restriction

Extensibility may also involve restricting an existing Template.

For example:

```text

            General Template
            │
            ├── permits A
            │
            ├── permits B
            │
            └── permits C

            Specialized Template
            │
            ├── permits A
            │
            └── permits B

```

Restriction is valid only where permitted by the applicable Specialization and Constraint semantics.

A restriction must not violate the structural or semantic requirements of the source Template.

---

# 11. Extension Combination

Multiple extensibility mechanisms may be combined.

For example:

```text

            Template
            │
            ├── specializes  ─────►  Base Template
            │
            ├── composes     ─────►  Reusable Template
            │
            ├── defines      ─────►  Parameters
            │
            └── reuses       ─────►  Elements

```

Combination is permitted only when the resulting Template has an unambiguous interpretation.

Conflicting extensions must not produce an undefined Template structure.

---

# 12. Extensibility and Relationships

Extensibility mechanisms rely on Template Relationships.

Examples include:

```text

    Specialization
        Derived Template
        │
        └── specializes  ─────►  Base Template

    Composition
        Template A
        │
        └── composes  ─────►  Template B

    Reuse
        Template A
        │
        └── references  ─────►  Reusable Element

```

Relationship semantics are defined by DF-TPL-009.

Extensibility does not redefine relationship semantics.

---

# 13. Extensibility and Constraints

Extensions are subject to Template Constraints.

Constraints may restrict:

* which Templates may be specialized;
* which Templates may be composed;
* which Elements may be reused;
* which parameters may be defined;
* which structural extensions are permitted.

Conceptually:

```text

            Extension
            │
            └── subject to  ─────►  Template Constraints

```

An extension that violates an applicable constraint is non-conformant.

The definition of constraints remains the responsibility of DF-TPL-010.

---

# 14. Extensibility and Validation

Template Validation evaluates whether an extension conforms to its applicable Template definition and constraints.

Conceptually:

```text

            Template Extension
                    │
                    ▼

           Template Validation
           │
           ├── Conformant
           │
           ├── Non-Conformant
           │
           └── Indeterminate

```

Extensibility defines what mechanisms may be used.

Validation determines whether their resulting structure conforms.

---

# 15. Extensibility and Lifecycle

An extension participates in the lifecycle of the Template in which it is defined.

Changes to an extension may result in a new Template Version.

For example:

```text

            Template Version 1
            │
            └── Extension A

            Template Version 2
            │
            ├── Extension A
            │
            └── Extension B

```

Template Lifecycle remains defined by DF-TPL-006.

Extensibility does not introduce an independent lifecycle for extensions.

---

# 18. Extension Traceability

An extension must be traceable to its source definition.

For example:

```text

            Base Template
            │
            └── source of  ─────►  Specialized Template

```

Similarly:

```text

            Reusable Element
            │
            └── source of  ─────►  Element reuse

```

Traceability supports:

* impact analysis;
* validation;
* governance;
* maintenance;
* controlled evolution;
* historical preservation.

---

# 20. Extensibility Boundaries

Template extensibility must remain within the responsibility boundaries of the Templates component.

It must not be used to extend or redefine:

| External Responsibility     | Boundary                                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Metadata**                | Metadata semantics remain defined by Metadata                 |
| **Document Identity**       | Identity semantics remain defined by Document Identity        |
| **Classification**          | Classification semantics remain defined by Classification     |
| **Workflow**                | Workflow behavior remains defined by Workflow                 |
| **Governance**              | Governance decisions remain defined by Template Governance    |
| **Validation**              | Conformance evaluation remains defined by Template Validation |
| **Repository**              | Physical organization remains outside Templates               |

Templates may define structural requirements concerning these components without assuming their responsibilities.

---

# 21. Extensibility Invariants

The following invariants apply to Template Extensibility.

### 21.1. Invariant 1 — Explicit Mechanism

Every extension must use an explicitly defined extensibility mechanism.

### 21.2. Invariant 2 — Source Traceability

Every specialization, composition, or reuse relationship must have an identifiable source.

### 21.3. Invariant 3 — Semantic Clarity

An extension must have an unambiguous semantic interpretation.

### 21.4. Invariant 4 — Constraint Conformance

Extensions must remain subject to applicable Template Constraints.

### 21.5. Invariant 5 — Validation

Extensions must be evaluable through Template Validation.

### 21.6. Invariant 6 — Version Distinction

An extension must not be confused with a Template Version.

### 21.7. Invariant 7 — No Implicit Modification

An extension must not silently modify unrelated existing definitions.

### 21.8. Invariant 8 — Responsibility Separation

Extensions must not redefine responsibilities belonging to other Documentation Framework components.

### 21.9. Invariant 9 — Technology Independence

Extensibility semantics must not depend on implementation technology.

### 21.10. Invariant 10 — Controlled Evolution

Changes to extensions must remain subject to the applicable Template Lifecycle and Governance rules.

# 23. Extensibility Model Summary

Template Extensibility provides controlled mechanisms for adapting and reusing Template definitions.

The principal mechanisms are:

```text

            Template Extensibility
            │
            ├── Specialization
            │
            ├── Composition
            │
            ├── Parameterization
            │
            ├── Element Reuse
            │
            └── Structural Extension

```

The mechanisms have distinct purposes:

| Mechanism                | Primary Purpose                      |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| **Specialization**       | Derive a more specific Template      |
| **Composition**          | Combine reusable Template structures |
| **Parameterization**     | Control defined structural variation |
| **Element Reuse**        | Reuse existing Template Elements     |
| **Structural Extension** | Add explicitly defined structure     |

Extensibility therefore provides reuse and controlled variation without weakening the conceptual boundaries established by the Templates architecture.

# 2. General Principles

Template design should follow the following principles:

1. Prefer reuse over duplication.
2. Keep semantics explicit.
3. Keep structure predictable.
4. Separate structural concerns from operational concerns.
5. Use the simplest mechanism that satisfies the requirement.
6. Avoid unnecessary specialization.
7. Avoid unnecessary composition.
8. Keep constraints explicit.
9. Preserve traceability.
10. Evolve Templates in a controlled manner.

---

# 4. Structural Practices

## 4.1. Use Consistent Section Organization

Sections should have predictable purposes.

Related Elements should be grouped into meaningful Sections rather than distributed arbitrarily throughout a Template.

## 4.2. Keep Structural Hierarchies Shallow

Deep nesting should be avoided unless it provides meaningful structural semantics.

For example:

```text

            Template
            │
            └── Section
                │
                └── Subsection
                    │
                    └── Element

```

should not be extended unnecessarily merely to represent formatting preferences.

## 4.3. Make Ordering Explicit

When Element or Section order has semantic significance, that ordering should be explicitly represented.

Ordering should not depend on accidental implementation behavior.

## 4.4. Distinguish Required and Optional Structure

Required and optional Elements should be explicitly distinguishable.

For example:

```text

            Section
            │
            ├── Required Element
            │
            └── Optional Element

```

Optionality should not be inferred from the absence of a constraint.

---

# 5. Element Practices

## 5.1. Reuse Existing Elements

Existing reusable Template Elements should be preferred over creating equivalent new Elements.

Before creating a new Element, determine whether an existing Element already provides the required semantics.

## 5.2. Avoid Overloaded Elements

An Element should have a clear purpose.

An Element that represents several unrelated concepts should normally be decomposed.

## 5.3. Preserve Element Semantics

When reusing an Element, its established semantics should be preserved.

A Template may constrain its use without silently redefining the Element itself.

## 5.4. Keep Element Names Consistent

Equivalent Elements should use consistent terminology throughout the Template ecosystem.

Different names should not be introduced for semantically identical Elements without justification.

---

# 6. Relationship Practices

## 6.1. Use the Most Specific Relationship

When defining a relationship, select the relationship type that most accurately represents its semantics.

For example:

```text

    Reference
    Dependency
    Composition
    Specialization
    Association

```

should not be used interchangeably.

## 6.2. Avoid Implicit Relationships

Relationships should be explicitly represented when they are relevant to Template semantics.

Do not rely on:

* naming conventions;
* physical location;
* file ordering;
* implementation-specific behavior

to establish semantic relationships.

## 6.3. Avoid Unnecessary Relationships

Not every connection between Template entities needs to become a formal relationship.

A relationship should be defined when its semantics provide meaningful structural, reuse, dependency, or traceability value.

# 7. Constraint Practices

## 7.1. Make Constraints Explicit

Constraints should clearly identify:

* their target;
* their semantic purpose;
* their scope;
* their applicability.

## 7.2. Prefer Simple Constraints

A simple constraint is preferable to a complex combination of interacting constraints when both achieve the same result.

## 7.3. Avoid Conflicting Constraints

Constraints applying to the same structural context should have a deterministic combined interpretation.

Conflicting constraints should be resolved before a Template is considered conformant.

## 7.4. Do Not Use Constraints as Documentation

A constraint should express an actual restriction or condition.

Descriptive information that does not restrict Template behavior should not be represented as a constraint.

# 8. Extensibility Practices

## 8.1. Prefer Reuse Before Specialization

When a Template can satisfy a requirement through reuse or composition, unnecessary specialization should be avoided.

## 8.2. Specialize for Meaningful Semantic Differences

Specialization should be used when the derived Template represents a meaningful specialization of an existing Template.

It should not be used merely to create a slightly different arrangement.

## 8.3. Compose Reusable Structures

Composition should be preferred when independently reusable structures can be combined without establishing a specialization relationship.

## 8.4. Parameterize Controlled Variation

Parameters should be used when variation is:

* predictable;
* explicitly definable;
* reusable;
* structurally meaningful.

Parameters should not be introduced merely to avoid creating a clear Template structure.

## 9.2. Minimize Breaking Changes

When evolving a Template, prefer changes that preserve existing conformance and usage where practical.

Potentially disruptive changes should receive explicit impact assessment.

# 10. Validation Practices

## 10.1. Validate Structural Conformance

Templates should be validated against their defined structure.

Validation should consider, as applicable:

* Elements;
* Sections;
* ordering;
* occurrences;
* parameters;
* relationships;
* constraints.

## 10.2. Validate Cross-Template Dependencies

Where Templates depend on or compose other Templates, their relationships should be evaluated for conformance.

## 10.3. Treat Indeterminate Results Explicitly

An inability to determine conformance should not automatically be interpreted as conformance.

The validation result should explicitly distinguish:

```text

    Conformant
    Non-Conformant
    Indeterminate

```

## 11.3. Separate Review from Validation

Validation evidence should support governance decisions, but validation and governance remain separate responsibilities.

---

# 12. Reuse Practices

Template reuse should be evaluated before introducing a new Template.

A useful decision sequence is:

```text

                    Required Structure
                            │
                            ▼

                    Existing Template?
                            │
                ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                │                       │
               Yes                      No
                │                       │
                ▼                       ▼

              Reuse             Existing reusable
                                    Elements?
                                        │
                                    Yes / No
                                        │
                                        ▼

                                Compose or create

```

The objective is to minimize unnecessary duplication while preserving semantic clarity.

# 15. Anti-Patterns

The following practices should generally be avoided.

### 15.1. Template Duplication

Creating a new Template when an existing Template can be reused or appropriately specialized.

### 15.2. Implicit Semantics

Relying on naming, ordering, or physical location to establish meaning that should be explicitly represented.

### 15.3. Over-Parameterization

Introducing large numbers of parameters to represent variations that would be clearer as separate Templates.

### 15.4. Over-Specialization

Creating deep specialization hierarchies without meaningful semantic distinctions.

### 15.5. Uncontrolled Composition

Composing Templates without clearly defined structural or semantic relationships.

### 15.6. Constraint Accumulation

Continuously adding constraints to compensate for an unclear Template structure.

### 15.7. Responsibility Leakage

Using Templates to define metadata, identity, classification, workflow, repository, or governance semantics.

### 15.8. Technology Coupling

Defining Template semantics in terms of a specific file format, database, programming language, or document editor.

# 17. Best Practices Summary

The principal Template best practices can be summarized as:

```text

            Design
            │
            ├── Define purpose
            │
            ├── Keep boundaries clear
            │
            └── Prefer simplicity

            Structure
            │
            ├── Organize consistently
            │
            ├── Make ordering explicit
            │
            └── Distinguish required/optional structure

            Reuse
            │
            ├── Reuse Elements
            │
            ├── Reuse Templates
            │
            ├── Compose when appropriate
            │
            └── Specialize when semantically justified

            Constraints
            │
            ├── Keep restrictions explicit
            │
            ├── Avoid conflicts
            │
            └── Avoid unnecessary complexity

            Evolution
            │
            ├── Version explicitly
            │
            ├── Preserve traceability
            │
            ├── Assess impact
            │
            └── Govern significant changes

            Validation
            │
            ├── Validate conformance
            │
            ├── Validate relationships
            │
            └── Treat indeterminate results explicitly

```

The central principle is:

> **Prefer explicit, reusable, simple, and semantically stable Template structures over duplicated, implicit, or unnecessarily complex structures.**

# 2. Dictionary Conventions

The following conventions apply.

### 2.1. Term

The canonical name of a concept.

### 2.2. Definition

The authoritative concise meaning of the term within the Templates component.

### 2.3. Related Terms

Terms that have a direct semantic relationship with the defined term.

### 2.4. Responsibility

When necessary, the responsible Template concept or document is identified.

# 3. Core Template Terms

| Term                        | Definition                                                                                                            | Related Terms                                        |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Template**                | A reusable structural definition for creating and representing documentation of a defined kind.                       | Template Type, Template Structure, Template Instance |
| **Template Type**           | A classification of Templates according to their defined structural or semantic purpose.                              | Template                                             |
| **Template Structure**      | The conceptual organization of Sections and Elements that defines the structure of a Template.                        | Template Section, Template Element                   |
| **Template Schema**         | The formal structural representation of a Template definition.                                                        | Template Model, Template Constraint                  |
| **Template Instance**       | A concrete application of a Template to create or represent a specific documentation structure.                       | Template, Document Instance                          |
| **Template Version**        | A version of a Template definition representing a controlled stage of its evolution.                                  | Template Lifecycle, Template Governance              |
| **Template Parameter**      | A defined variable of a Template that permits controlled structural or contextual variation.                          | Parameterization, Template Instance                  |
| **Template Constraint**     | An explicit restriction or condition applicable to a Template entity or relationship.                                 | Constraint, Template Validation                      |
| **Template Relationship**   | An explicitly defined semantic or structural relationship between Template entities.                                  | Composition, Specialization, Reference               |
| **Template Specialization** | A Template derived from another Template to provide a more specific definition.                                       | Specialization Relationship                          |
| **Template Composition**    | The incorporation of reusable Template structures into another Template.                                              | Composition Relationship                             |
| **Template Conformance**    | The condition in which a Template or Template Instance satisfies its applicable structural and semantic requirements. | Template Validation                                  |

| Term                       | Definition                                                                                  | Related Terms                            |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |

| **Template Element**       | A fundamental structural unit used within a Template Structure.                             | Section, Element Category                |
| **Structural Element**     | A Template Element whose primary purpose is to represent structural organization.           | Template Element                         |
| **Content Element**        | A Template Element intended to represent a location or structure for documentation content. | Template Element                         |
| **Reference Element**      | A Template Element intended to represent a reference to another defined entity or resource. | Template Element, Reference Relationship |
| **Metadata Element**       | A Template Element that provides a structural location for Metadata information.            | Metadata, Template Element               |

# 10. Governance Terms

# 11. Extensibility Terms

# 12. Conformance Terms

# 13. Terms That Must Remain Distinct

The following terms represent important semantic distinctions.

| Term A                     | Term B                            | Distinction                                                                                              |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Template**               | **Template Instance**             | A Template defines reusable structure; an Instance applies that structure.                               |
| **Template**               | **Template Version**              | A Template is the conceptual definition; a Version represents a controlled stage of its evolution.       |
| **Template Version**       | **Document Revision**             | Template Version concerns Template evolution; Document Revision concerns a document.                     |
| **Template Structure**     | **Physical Repository Structure** | Template Structure is conceptual; repository organization is external to Templates.                      |
| **Template Schema**        | **Template Model**                | The Model defines conceptual relationships; the Schema represents the structure formally.                |
| **Constraint**             | **Validation**                    | A Constraint defines a restriction; Validation evaluates conformance.                                    |
| **Governance**             | **Validation**                    | Governance controls change and approval; Validation evaluates conformance.                               |
| **Composition**            | **Specialization**                | Composition combines reusable structures; Specialization derives a more specific Template.               |
| **Reference**              | **Composition**                   | A Reference links to another entity; Composition incorporates reusable structure.                        |
| **Dependency**             | **Specialization**                | Dependency expresses reliance; Specialization expresses derivation.                                      |
| **Metadata Element**       | **Metadata**                      | A Metadata Element provides structural placement; Metadata defines metadata semantics.                   |
| **Identity Element**       | **Document Identity**             | An Identity Element provides structural placement; Document Identity defines identity semantics.         |
| **Classification Element** | **Classification**                | A Classification Element provides structural placement; Classification defines classification semantics. |

---

# 14. Canonical Terminology

The following terms are the preferred canonical terms within the Templates component:

* **Template**
* **Template Type**
* **Template Structure**
* **Template Section**
* **Template Element**
* **Template Schema**
* **Template Instance**
* **Template Parameter**
* **Template Constraint**
* **Template Relationship**
* **Template Version**
* **Template Specialization**
* **Template Composition**
* **Template Conformance**
* **Template Lifecycle**
* **Template Validation**
* **Template Governance**
* **Template Extensibility**

Equivalent informal terms should not replace these terms in normative Template documentation when the canonical term is applicable.

---

# 15. Terminology Usage Rules

### 15.1. Rule 1 — Template

Use **Template** for the reusable structural definition.

Do not use **Template** to refer to a concrete document instance.

### 15.2. Rule 2 — Template Instance

Use **Template Instance** for a concrete application of a Template.

### 15.3. Rule 3 — Template Version

Use **Template Version** for controlled evolution of a Template definition.

Do not use **Revision**, **Edition**, or **Baseline** as synonyms.

### 15.4. Rule 4 — Constraint

Use **Constraint** for a restriction or condition.

Do not use **Validation** as a synonym.

### 15.5. Rule 5 — Relationship

Use the most specific relationship category available when the semantics are known.

### 15.6. Rule 6 — Composition

Use **Composition** only when one Template incorporates another reusable Template structure.

### 15.7. Rule 7 — Specialization

Use **Specialization** only when a Template is derived as a more specific definition from another Template.

### 15.8. Rule 8 — Reuse

Use **Reuse** for explicit reuse of existing Template definitions or Elements.

Do not infer reuse merely from similar structures.

### 15.9. Rule 9 — Extensibility

Use **Extensibility** for mechanisms that permit controlled adaptation or reuse.

### 15.10. Rule 10 — Conformance

Use **Conformance** for satisfaction of applicable Template requirements.

## 1.1. Purpose

This document defines the normative specification of the **Templates Component** of the Documentation Framework.

It consolidates the architectural, conceptual, structural, behavioral, and extensibility requirements established by the Templates documentation and provides a canonical reference for Template conformance.

The specification defines what a Template is, how Templates are structurally represented, how their elements and relationships are defined, how constraints are expressed, and how Templates are versioned, instantiated, validated, governed, and extended.

This document does not replace the detailed Templates documents. It provides their normative synthesis and establishes the requirements that implementations and dependent Documentation Framework components must respect.

---

# 2. Normative Language

The following terms are used with their normative meaning:

* **MUST** — a mandatory requirement.
* **MUST NOT** — a mandatory prohibition.
* **SHOULD** — a recommended requirement that may be omitted only for a justified reason.
* **SHOULD NOT** — a recommendation against a practice that may be used only for a justified reason.
* **MAY** — an optional capability.

Requirements in this document apply to conformant Template definitions and Template implementations within the scope of the Documentation Framework.

---

# 4. Template Structural Model

The canonical Template structural model is:

```text

            Template
            │
            ├── Template Type
            │
            ├── Template Structure
            │   │
            │   └── Template Section
            │       │
            │       └── Template Element
            │
            ├── Template Schema
            │
            ├── Template Parameter
            │
            ├── Template Constraint
            │
            ├── Template Relationship
            │
            └── Template Version

```

A conformant Template MUST preserve the distinctions represented by this model.

The Template Model defines the conceptual relationships between these entities.

The Template Schema defines their structural representation.

The Template Constraints define what is permitted.

Template Validation determines whether a Template conforms to its applicable requirements.

---

# 5. Template Type

A **Template Type** identifies the conceptual category of a Template.

Template Types provide semantic classification of Templates without replacing the Classification Component.

A Template MUST be associated with a Template Type where such association is required by the applicable Template Schema.

Template Types MUST NOT be used to redefine document Classification.

---

# 8. Template Elements

A **Template Element** is an identifiable structural or content-bearing component of a Template.

The canonical Template Element categories are:

```text

            Template Element
            │
            ├── Structural Element
            │
            ├── Content Element
            │
            ├── Reference Element
            │
            ├── Metadata Element
            │
            ├── Identity Element
            │
            ├── Classification Element
            │
            ├── Parameterized Element
            │
            └── Reusable Element

```

A Template Element MUST have a defined purpose within its Template Structure.

Template Elements MAY be:

* mandatory or optional;
* singular or repeated;
* ordered;
* parameterized;
* reusable;
* constrained;
* related to other elements.

Metadata Elements, Identity Elements, and Classification Elements provide structural locations or requirements for information belonging to their respective components.

They MUST NOT redefine the semantics of:

* Metadata;
* Document Identity;
* Classification.

---

# 13. Template Composition

**Template Composition** defines the construction of a Template through the combination of existing Template structures or reusable Template Elements.

Composition SHOULD be used to promote:

* reuse;
* consistency;
* modularity;
* controlled structural construction.

Composition MUST preserve the semantic identity of the participating Templates and Elements.

Composition MUST NOT be used merely to create implicit dependencies.

Composition Constraints MAY restrict which Templates or Elements can participate in a composition.

---

# 16. Template Instance

A **Template Instance** is a concrete application of a Template.

A Template Instance represents the use of a Template definition to establish the structure of a concrete documentation artifact.

The distinction MUST be preserved:

```text

            Template
            │
            └── defines reusable structure

            Template Version
            │
            └── identifies a particular Template definition version

            Template Instance
            │
            └── represents a concrete application of the Template

```

A Template Instance MUST NOT redefine the Template itself.

Template Instance management MUST NOT be confused with Document Instance lifecycle management.

---

# 17. Template Lifecycle

A Template MUST follow the applicable Template Lifecycle.

The canonical lifecycle states are:

```text

                  Draft
                    │
                    ▼

                 Defined
                    │
                    ▼

                  Active
                    │
                    ▼

                Deprecated
                    │
                    ▼

                 Retired

```

Additional permitted transitions include:

```text

    Defined     ─────►  Draft
    Deprecated  ─────►  Active
    Active      ─────►  Retired

```

Lifecycle state and Template Version MUST remain distinct.

Lifecycle state identifies the current lifecycle condition of a Template.

Template Version identifies a particular version of its definition.

Retirement MUST NOT imply automatic deletion or loss of historical information.

Historical Template definitions SHOULD be preserved when required for traceability, conformance, or knowledge preservation.

---

# 21. Cross-Component Compatibility

Templates interact with other Documentation Layer components while remaining responsible only for Template concerns.

## 21.1. Metadata

Templates MAY define locations and requirements for Metadata through Metadata Elements.

Templates MUST NOT define Metadata semantics.

Metadata compatibility MAY be evaluated during Template Validation.

---

## 21.2. Document Identity

Templates MAY define structural locations and requirements for Document Identity information through Identity Elements.

Templates MUST NOT define Document Identity semantics.

Document Identity compatibility MAY be evaluated during Template Validation.

---

## 21.3. Classification

Templates MAY define structural locations and requirements for Classification information through Classification Elements.

Templates MUST NOT define Classification semantics.

Classification compatibility MAY be evaluated during Template Validation.

---

## 21.4. Workflow

Workflow MAY use Template lifecycle and validation information.

Templates MUST NOT define document workflow.

---

## 21.5. Registry

The Registry MAY reference Templates and Template Versions.

Templates MUST NOT define registry management.

---

## 21.6. Automation

Automation MAY use Template definitions for:

* validation;
* generation;
* metadata placement;
* structural generation;
* consistency verification.

Automation MUST consume Template semantics rather than redefine them.

---

---

# 23. Canonical Abstract Template Definition

The canonical abstract representation of a Template is:

```text

            Template
            │
            ├── Type
            │
            ├── Structure
            │   │
            │   └── Sections
            │       │
            │       └── Elements
            │
            ├── Schema
            │
            ├── Parameters
            │
            ├── Constraints
            │
            ├── Relationships
            │
            └── Version

```

Behavioral and governance aspects associated with the Template are:

```text

            Template
            │
            ├── Lifecycle
            │
            ├── Validation
            │
            ├── Governance
            │
            └── Extensibility

```

This abstract representation is normative at the conceptual level.

It does not prescribe a physical or technological representation.

---

# 24. Normative Invariants

The following invariants MUST be preserved.

### 24.1. Template Identity

A Template MUST remain distinguishable from its Template Instance and Template Version.

### 24.2. Structural Separation

Template Structure MUST remain distinct from physical repository structure.

### 24.3. Model and Schema Separation

Template Model MUST remain distinct from Template Schema.

### 24.4. Constraint and Validation Separation

Template Constraints MUST remain distinct from Template Validation.

### 24.5. Lifecycle and Governance Separation

Template Lifecycle MUST remain distinct from Template Governance.

### 24.6. Composition and Specialization Separation

Template Composition MUST remain distinct from Template Specialization.

### 24.7. Cross-Component Responsibility

Metadata, Document Identity, and Classification semantics MUST remain outside the Templates Component.

### 24.8. Technology Independence

The conceptual Template definition MUST NOT depend on a specific implementation technology, programming language, storage mechanism, or serialization format.

### 24.9. Traceability

Template Versions, validation results, governance decisions, and significant Template changes MUST remain traceable where applicable.

### 24.10. Controlled Evolution

Template evolution MUST occur through controlled and explicitly defined mechanisms.

## 1.1. Purpose

This document provides representative examples of Templates defined according to the Documentation Framework Templates Component.

The examples demonstrate how the concepts, structures, elements, parameters, constraints, relationships, composition, specialization, versioning, lifecycle, validation, and governance mechanisms defined by the Templates Component may be applied.

The examples are illustrative and are not themselves normative Template definitions unless explicitly adopted and governed as such.

---

# 2. Example Conventions

The examples use the following notation:

```text

    [TEMPLATE]
        Template definition

    [SECTION]
        Template Section

    [ELEMENT]
        Template Element

    [PARAMETER]
        Template Parameter

    [CONSTRAINT]
        Template Constraint

    [RELATIONSHIP]
        Template Relationship

```

The notation is illustrative and does not constitute a required serialization format.

---

# 3. Basic Template Example

A simple Template may define the structure of a technical document.

```text

    Template: Technical Document

    Type:
        Technical Documentation

    Structure:
        Section: Introduction
            Element: Purpose
            Element: Scope

        Section: Main Content
            Element: Content

        Section: References
            Element: Related Documents

```

This Template defines reusable documentation structure without defining how the resulting document is stored.

---

# 4. Structured Template Example

A more detailed Template may define a document with several mandatory and optional elements.

```text

    Template: Architecture Document

    Structure:

        Section: Metadata
            Element: Document Identifier
            Element: Title
            Element: Status
            Element: Version
            Element: Revision

        Section: Introduction
            Element: Purpose
            Element: Scope

        Section: Architecture
            Element: Architectural Position
            Element: Components
            Element: Relationships
            Element: Constraints

        Section: Governance
            Element: Responsibilities
            Element: Governance Rules

        Section: References
            Element: Related Documents

```

The Template defines the expected structure while the semantics of Metadata and Document Identity remain the responsibility of their respective components.

---

# 5. Optional Element Example

A Template may contain optional elements.

```text

    Section: References

        Element: Related Documents
            Occurrence: Optional

        Element: External References
            Occurrence: Optional

```

The optionality is a Template structural property.

It does not determine whether a particular document is complete unless the applicable Template Constraints establish such a requirement.

---

# 6. Repeated Element Example

A Template Element may occur multiple times.

```text

    Section: Requirements

        Element: Requirement
            Occurrence: One or More

```

A Template Instance may therefore contain:

```text

    Requirement 1
    Requirement 2
    Requirement 3
...

```

The Template defines the permitted occurrence model; the Template Instance contains the concrete occurrences.

---

# 7. Ordered Element Example

A Template may explicitly define ordering.

```text

    Section: Document Structure

        1. Purpose
        2. Scope
        3. Concepts
        4. Architecture
        5. Constraints
        6. References

```

Ordering is part of the Template Structure.

An implementation MUST preserve the semantic ordering requirements established by the Template Schema and applicable Constraints.

---

# 8. Parameterized Template Example

A Template may use parameters to support controlled variation.

```text

    Template: Component Document

    Parameter:
        ComponentName

    Parameter:
        ComponentPurpose

    Structure:

        Section: Introduction
            Element: Component Name
                Parameter: ComponentName

            Element: Purpose
                Parameter: ComponentPurpose

        Section: Architecture
            Element: Architectural Position

        Section: References
            Element: Related Documents

```

The Template remains the same while parameter values vary between Template Instances.

For example:

```text

    ComponentName     =  Templates
    ComponentPurpose  =  Define reusable documentation structures

```

and:

```text

    ComponentName     =  Metadata
    ComponentPurpose  =  Define document metadata

```

Parameterization provides controlled variation without duplicating the complete Template.

---

# 9. Reusable Element Example

A reusable Template Element may be defined independently and incorporated into multiple Templates.

```text

    Reusable Element:
        Document Status

    Purpose:
        Represents the status information required by applicable documentation.

    Used by:
        Technical Document Template
        Architecture Document Template
        Component Document Template

```

Reuse promotes consistency and reduces duplicated structural definitions.

The reusable Element remains subject to the Constraints and Schema of each Template in which it is used.

---

# 10. Composition Example

A Template may be constructed from existing reusable structures.

```text

    Template: Component Architecture Document

    Composition:

        ├── Common Document Structure
        │
        ├── Architecture Structure
        │
        └── Reference Structure

```

Conceptually:

```text

            Component Architecture Document
            │
            ├── Common Document Structure
            │
            ├── Architecture Structure
            │
            └── Reference Structure

```

Composition combines existing structures.

It does not imply that one Template is a specialization of another.

---

# 11. Specialization Example

A general Template may be specialized for a more specific purpose.

```text

    Base Template:
        Technical Document

    Specialized Template:
        Architecture Document

```

The specialization may refine the base structure:

```text

            Technical Document
            │
            ├── Introduction
            │
            ├── Main Content
            │
            └── References
                    │
                    ▼

          Architecture Document
          │
          ├── Introduction
          │
          ├── Architectural Position
          │
          ├── Components
          │
          ├── Relationships
          │
          ├── Constraints
          │
          └── References

```

The Architecture Document remains semantically related to the Technical Document while providing a more specific structure.

---

# 12. Constraint Example

A Template may require specific structural conditions.

```text

    Template Constraint:

        Every Architecture Document MUST contain:

            Purpose
            Scope
            Architectural Position
            Components
            Relationships

```

Another constraint may restrict occurrence:

```text

    Occurrence Constraint:

        Purpose
            Minimum occurrence: 1
            Maximum occurrence: 1

```

A parameter constraint may define a requirement for a parameter:

```text

    Parameter Constraint:

        ComponentName
            MUST have a non-empty value

```

Constraints define what is permitted.

Validation determines whether the resulting Template definition satisfies those constraints.

---

# 13. Relationship Example

A Template may define relationships between its elements.

```text

    Template Relationship:

        Component
        │
        └── contains  ─────►  Component Responsibility

```

A different relationship may reference another Template:

```text

    Template Relationship:

        Architecture Document Template
        │
        └── references  ─────►  Architecture Concepts Template

```

The relationship type MUST be explicitly identified.

A reference MUST NOT automatically be interpreted as composition.

---

# 14. Cross-Template Dependency Example

A Template may depend on another Template.

```text

    Template A:
        Component Architecture Document

    Dependency:
        Architecture Concepts Template

```

The dependency indicates that Template A relies on concepts or structures provided by Template B.

The dependency does not imply:

* composition;
* specialization;
* inheritance.

These remain distinct relationship semantics.

---

# 15. Template Version Example

A Template may evolve through multiple versions.

```text

    Template:
        Architecture Document

    Version 1.0:
        Introduction
        Architecture
        References

    Version 2.0:
        Introduction
        Architecture
        Governance
        References

```

The versions represent different definitions of the same Template.

A Template Version MUST NOT be interpreted as a Document Revision.

---

# 16. Template Instance Example

A Template Instance represents the application of a Template.

Given:

```text

    Template:
        Component Document

```

with:

```text

    ComponentName     =  Templates
    ComponentPurpose  =  Define reusable documentation structures

```

a corresponding Template Instance may conceptually produce:

```text

    Component Document

        Component Name:
            Templates

        Purpose:
            Define reusable documentation structures

        Architecture:
            ...

        References:
            ...

```

The concrete values belong to the Template Instance.

The reusable structure remains defined by the Template.

---

# 17. Lifecycle Example

A newly created Template may progress through its lifecycle:

```text

                  Draft
                    │
                    ▼

                 Defined
                    │
                    ▼

                  Active

```

When replacement becomes necessary:

```text

                  Active
                    │
                    ▼

                Deprecated
                    │
                    ▼

                 Retired

```

A deprecated Template may be reactivated where governance permits:

```text

                Deprecated
                    │
                    ▼

                  Active

```

Lifecycle transitions MUST comply with the applicable governance requirements.

---

# 18. Validation Example

Consider the following Template:

```text

    Template:
        Architecture Document

    Required Elements:

        Purpose
        Scope
        Architecture
        References

```

Validation may produce:

```text

    Structural Validation:
        Conformant

    Element Validation:
        Conformant

    Schema Validation:
        Conformant

    Constraint Validation:
        Non-Conformant

    Result:
        Non-Conformant

```

The validation finding may identify:

```text

    Missing required element:
        Scope

```

The validation result does not itself approve or reject the Template.

Governance remains responsible for the corresponding governance decision.

---

# 19. Governance Example

A proposed Template change may follow:

```text

             Template Change
                    │
                    ▼

            Change Assessment
                    │
                    ▼

             Template Review
                    │
                    ▼

                Validation
                    │
                    ▼

           Governance Decision
           │
           ├── Accepted
           │
           ├── Rejected
           │
           ├── Deferred
           │
           └── Returned for Revision

```

Validation provides evidence for the governance process.

It does not replace the governance decision.

---

# 20. Compatibility Example

A Template may define a location for document identity information:

```text

    Section: Document Identity

        Element: Document Identifier
        Element: Edition
        Element: Revision

```

The Template establishes where the information is structurally represented.

The semantics of:

* Document Identifier;
* Edition;
* Revision

remain defined by the Document Identity Component.

Similarly, a Template may contain:

```text

    Section: Metadata

        Element: Author
        Element: Status
        Element: Language

```

without redefining Metadata semantics.

---

# 21. Combined Example

The following example combines several Template mechanisms.

```text

    Template:
        Component Architecture Document

    Type:
        Architecture Documentation

    Version:
        2.0

    Structure:

        Section: Metadata
            Element: Document Metadata

        Section: Introduction
            Element: Purpose
            Element: Scope

        Section: Architecture
            Element: Architectural Position
            Element: Components
            Element: Relationships

        Section: Constraints
            Element: Architectural Constraints

        Section: References
            Element: Related Documents
                Occurrence: Zero or More

    Parameters:

        ComponentName
        ComponentPurpose

    Relationships:

        references  ─────►  Architecture Concepts Template
        references  ─────►  Architecture Model Template

    Constraints:

        Purpose MUST occur exactly once
        Scope MUST occur exactly once
        ComponentName MUST be provided
        Related Documents MAY occur multiple times

```

This example demonstrates:

* Template Type;
* Template Structure;
* Template Sections;
* Template Elements;
* Template Parameters;
* Template Relationships;
* Template Constraints;
* Template Version;
* compatibility with other Templates.

---

# 22. Example of Controlled Specialization

A generic component Template may be specialized into several documentation Templates.

```text

            Component Template
            │
            ├── Component Architecture Template
            │
            ├── Component Structure Template
            │
            ├── Component Behavior Template
            │
            └── Component Reference Template

```

Each specialization may retain common structural elements while introducing domain-specific structure.

This approach avoids duplicating common Template definitions.

---

# 23. Example of Template Reuse

A common reusable structure may be used across several Templates:

```text

    Reusable Structure:
        Standard Introduction

    Contains:
        Purpose
        Scope

```

It may be composed into:

```text

    Architecture Document Template
    Component Document Template
    Reference Document Template
    Specification Document Template

```

The shared structure promotes consistency across documentation types.

---

# 24. Example of Template Conformance

A Template may be evaluated against its requirements.

```text

    Template:
        Component Architecture Document

    Schema:
        Conformant

    Elements:
        Conformant

    Parameters:
        Conformant

    Relationships:
        Conformant

    Constraints:
        Conformant

    Cross-Template Compatibility:
        Conformant

    Overall Conformance:
        Conformant

```

The conformance result applies to the evaluated Template definition and its applicable Template Version.

---

# 25. Example of Non-Conformance

A Template may fail conformance when it violates a mandatory requirement.

```text

    Template Constraint:

        Every Architecture Document MUST contain
        an Architectural Position Element.

```

Template definition:

```text

    Section: Architecture

        Element: Components
        Element: Relationships

```

Validation result:

```text

    Result:
        Non-Conformant

    Finding:
        Required Architectural Position Element is missing.

```

The finding identifies the violated requirement without changing the Template definition automatically.

---

# 26. Example of Template Evolution

A Template may evolve incrementally.

### 26.1. Version 1.0

```text

    Introduction
    Architecture
    References

```

### 26.2. Version 1.1

```text

    Introduction
    Architecture
    Constraints
    References

```

### 26.3. Version 2.0

```text

    Metadata
    Introduction
    Architecture
    Constraints
    Governance
    References

```

The exact versioning policy is determined by applicable Template Governance.

The examples illustrate the distinction between structural evolution and the lifecycle state of the Template.

---

### 26.1. Version 1.0

```text

    Introduction
    Architecture
    References

```

### 26.2. Version 1.1

```text

    Introduction
    Architecture
    Constraints
    References

```

### 26.3. Version 2.0

```text

    Metadata
    Introduction
    Architecture
    Constraints
    Governance
    References

```

The exact versioning policy is determined by applicable Template Governance.

The examples illustrate the distinction between structural evolution and the lifecycle state of the Template.

---

# 27. Example of Retired Template Preservation

A Template may become obsolete:

```text

    Template:
        Legacy Architecture Document

    Lifecycle:
        Retired

```

The Template definition may nevertheless be preserved because historical Document Instances were created using it.

Preservation allows historical documentation to remain understandable and traceable.

Retirement therefore does not imply deletion.

---

# 28. Example of a Minimal Template

A minimal valid Template may consist of:

```text

    Template:
        Simple Note

    Type:
        Note

    Structure:
        Section: Content
            Element: Text

    Version:
        1.0

```

Additional concepts such as Parameters, Relationships, Composition, or Specialization are not required when they are not applicable.

A Template SHOULD remain as simple as its intended purpose permits.

---

# 29. Example of a Complex Template

A complex Template may contain:

```text

            Template
            │
            ├── Type
            │
            ├── Structure
            │   │
            │   └── Sections
            │       │
            │       └── Elements
            │
            ├── Parameters
            │
            ├── Constraints
            │
            ├── Relationships
            │
            ├── Composition
            │
            ├── Specialization
            │
            ├── Version
            │
            ├── Lifecycle
            │
            ├── Validation
            │
            └── Governance

```

Complexity is justified only when required by the documentation purpose.

The existence of available Template mechanisms does not require every Template to use them.

---

# 30. Example Design Principles

The examples demonstrate several general principles.

## 30.1. Reuse Before Duplication

Existing structures and Elements SHOULD be reused whenever appropriate.

## 30.2. Explicit Semantics

Relationships, Constraints, Parameters, Composition, and Specialization SHOULD be explicit.

## 30.3. Controlled Variation

Parameters SHOULD be preferred over duplicated Templates when the variation is controlled and semantically equivalent.

## 30.4. Appropriate Specialization

Specialization SHOULD be used when a more specific Template retains a meaningful semantic relationship with a more general Template.

## 30.5. Appropriate Composition

Composition SHOULD be used when independent structures can be combined without implying specialization.

## 30.6. Simplicity

Templates SHOULD contain only the structural mechanisms required by their purpose.

## 30.7. Traceability

Significant Template evolution SHOULD remain traceable through Template Versions and applicable Governance records.

These mechanisms allow Templates to provide reusable, explicit, structured, and controlled documentation definitions while remaining independent of document storage, repository organization, and implementation technology.
